newsitem.title: FRANCE: French mediator launches new trucker talks.
newsitem.headline: French mediator launches new trucker talks.

text.p: The French government stepped into a truckers dispute on Sunday, naming a mediator to launch a new round of talks on seven-day blockades of many towns and petrol depots across the country.

Unions urged truckers, pressing for shorter working hours, wage hikes and retirement at 55 instead of 60, to hold fast in a protest which echoes a damaging 24-day rail strike a year ago that sent Prime Minister Alain Juppe's popularity plummeting.
Mediator Robert Cros, named by Transport Minister Bernard Pons a few hours earlier, opened a new round of talks at six p.m. (1700 GMT) with union officials and haulage bosses.

"We're here to settle grievances. Let's hope the bosses hvae changed their stance. If that is not the case we'll continue as long as is necessary," Alain Renault, of the Communist CGT union, told reporters.

Jehan Demarne, one of the haulage company representatives, said the mediator might "reach a balanced accord. There is no doubt that the state, according to what it brings to each side, can ensure a deal is reached."
Pons had named Cros after a third round of talks failed on Saturday. Until last year Cros presided a national conciliation commission set up after the last trucker's conflict in 1992.
"Cros's mandate is to obtain a balanced accord between the parties, given the unions' grievances and the economic situation of haulage companies," the ministry said in a statement.
"The State is determined to do its share to reach an accord," the ministry said. The government has agreed to help fund retirement at 55, according to unions.
Several unions threatened to harden the protest, which is weighing on the economy, unless he produced quick results.
"If there is no progress on Sunday, we don't rule out the possibility of spreading the movement to (school and other bus services)," Claude Debons of the pro-Socialist CFDT union said.
CFDT leader Nicole Notat has called a truckers' rally in Paris on Monday if talks failed to break the deadlock.
The Force Ouvriere union was more optimistic, saying that Pons was willing to help fund retirement at 55 but only as part of a general agreement solving the dispute.
The haulage companies said in a statement they had made as many concessions as they could, including retirement at 55 and full payment of all working hours, including time spent loading.

Socialist former Prime Minister Laurent Fabius said the strike was typical of France's unease. "The French are crushed by taxes, unemployment and by a feeling that the government despises them and says 'I have the solution, you don't understand anything," he told France-2 television.

Tens of thousands of trucks blocked main roads around 30 cities and a dozen fuel depots. Some blockades were eased but unions said this was only to give strikers a weekend break, and the screw would be tightened once again from later on Sunday.

The southwest, parts of the south and Normandy were all badly hit. Petrol stations have run out of fuel in areas of Normandy and the south-west around Bordeaux, the city which has Juppe as its mayor and is singled out for the toughest protests.

Several dozen truckers have blocked a motorway close to Paris's wholesale food market at Rungis but unions said they did not plan to seal off the market which handles two million tonnes of food supplies a day.

On the ring-road around Caen in Normandy, two people died and four were injured on Saturday evening when a car rammed a lorry which had been blockading the motorway. Police said the car had apparently skirted barriers sealing the road off.
